item.title: index
item.description: United States 1920–45 Wiki A narrative-research knowledge base on American history from the aftermath of the First World War through the end of the Second World War — normalcy and the 1920s boom, Prohibition and mass culture, the Great Depression, the New Deal, industrial and labor change, neutralit...

item.title: [source] The Peace Negotiations: A Personal Narrative (Lansing, 1921)
item.description: Robert Lansing's 1921 personal narrative of the Paris Peace Conference, written after Woodrow Wilson forced his resignation as Secretary of State in February 1920, setting out their differences over the League Covenant, Article 10, secret diplomacy, the lack of an American programme, Shantung, and the Treaty of Versailles.

item.title: [source] Barriers Down: The Story of the News Agency Epoch (Cooper, 1942)
item.description: Kent Cooper’s first-person insider history—as Associated Press traffic chief then general manager—of AP’s long fight to break the Reuters–Havas–Wolff news-agency cartel: South American entry, Japanese Rengo alliance, Geneva and London negotiations, emancipation from exclusive contracts, wartime propaganda frame, and the claim that truth and a free press are the best answer to government and monopoly news control.

item.title: [source] Overnight Success: Federal Express and Frederick Smith (Trimble, 1993)
item.description: Vance H. Trimble’s FedEx biography—Dixie Greyhound and Toddle House fortune of Frederick Smith’s father, Memphis East Parkway childhood, with Yale/Vietnam and overnight-network founding retained as forward continuity.

item.title: [source] Rickover: The Struggle for Excellence (Duncan, 2001)
item.description: Francis Duncan’s authorized biography of Adm. Hyman G. Rickover—Maków–Chicago origins, Naval Academy, destroyer and battleship duty, Columbia electrical engineering, submarines and marriage, Engineering Duty Only, Asiatic station, and BuShips Electrical Section leadership through World War II, with postwar nuclear-Navy chapters retained only as forward continuity.

item.title: [source] Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald’s (Kroc with Anderson, 1977)
item.description: Ray Kroc’s autobiography (with Robert Anderson)—early Lily Tulip paper-cup selling, Florida boom interlude, the 1927–37 cup-industry grind, and Multimixer entrepreneurship from 1938, with the 1954 McDonald’s franchise empire retained only as forward continuity.

item.title: [source] Vision: A Saga of the Sky (Mansfield, 1956)
item.description: Harold Mansfield’s narrative history of the Boeing Airplane Company from William E. Boeing’s 1910 Dominguez Field encounter through Claire Egtvedt, Phil Johnson, and Bill Allen—mail planes, pursuits, all-metal Monomail/247, Flying Fortress and B-29 Superfortress, Battle of Kansas, postwar swept-wing B-47/B-52, Stratocruiser, 707 jet transport, and Bomarc missiles—framed by engineer John Haberlin’s thirty-year banquet speech.

item.title: [source] The Snowball: Warren Buffett and the Business of Life (Schroeder, 2008)
item.description: Alice Schroeder’s authorized Buffett biography—Nebraska lineage, Omaha Depression childhood, Washington wartime paper routes and sales hustles, Philadelphia college, with postwar Graham/Berkshire chapters retained as forward continuity.

item.title: [source] Empire / Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness (Barlett & Steele, 1979)
item.description: Donald L. Barlett and James B. Steele’s investigative biography of Howard Hughes—from Hughes Tool inheritance, Hollywood extravagance, and 1930s aviation records through World War II defense contracts, the Spruce Goose, and the 1947 Senate investigation, then postwar RKO, TWA, Las Vegas, Watergate/Hughesgate, CIA Project Jennifer, and the 1976 death and estate fight.

item.title: [source] American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer (Bird and Sherwin, 2005/2006)
item.description: Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin’s Pulitzer-winning biography of J. Robert Oppenheimer—from New York childhood and European quantum training through Berkeley left politics, Los Alamos, Hiroshima aftermath, Institute for Advanced Study leadership, the hydrogen-bomb fight, and the 1954 AEC security hearing that destroyed his government career.
